units: a mold is built out of clay before the pouring
the molten metal is poured without a break
the piece cools for a whole night without being moved
the mold is broken once the metal has cooled
the surface looks reddish and unpolished when it comes out
a tuning specialist adjusts the pitch at the end of the process
material is taken off the inside to change the note
the craftsman adds a personal mark when the result satisfies him
text: The workshop heats up long before any metal moves. The founder starts by building a mold out of clay, building it up by hand, one layer over the last, then leaving it to dry beside the furnace. Once the alloy runs, he pours it in a single steady stream and watches the bubbles come up to the surface. Cooling takes the whole night after that, and nobody touches the piece until it has gone lukewarm. When the shell breaks under the mallet, out comes a coppery flank, reddish and still rough. The tuner works last. He strikes the rim, listens to the note, shaves thin curls off the inner wall, and strikes again. Every pass lifts the pitch a shade. Once the tone rings clear and the vibration dies away without a beat, the craftsman puts his tool down and cuts a small mark of his own into the metal.

units: shared places have grown too noisy
shops play music to hold on to their customers
household machines give off unpleasant sound signals
each source taken alone seems harmless
it is the sum of the sources that makes the din
concentration scatters and talking costs more effort
vulnerable people now stay away from public places
doctors report lasting exhaustion among those exposed
the writer holds that an individual answer would not work
the writer asks builders and manufacturers to protect quiet
text: One quiet shift deserves a moment of attention: the places we share have grown far too loud, and the fault is spread across many hands. Shops pipe in music tuned to keep customers browsing. Household machines announce every finished task with a shrill little tone. Taken one at a time, each of these sounds is harmless. Stacked together they build a roar that nobody ever chose. Attention breaks apart, a plain conversation costs more effort than it should, and the frailest users simply stop coming to public places. Clinicians report a lasting exhaustion among people who cannot step away from the racket. Because the cause is collective, no private remedy will do: plugging your ears only shifts the burden onto you. The people who design buildings and the firms that build our machines should treat quiet as a resource worth keeping.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she began her trade in a country workshop
her first specialty was mending cracked soundboards
the bodies she repaired gave a muffled sound
neither the wood nor the varnish nor the strings explained the fault
she blamed a layer of glue laid on too thickly
she tested hanging samples that she struck
the samples with the least glue sounded better
she changed her preparation and corrected the instruments already delivered
she passes this method on to students who come from far away
text: The woman who restores old instruments learned her trade in a country workshop, where most of her work was mending cracked soundboards. One puzzle held her for whole seasons: the bodies she glued back together came out muffled, as though a blanket lay over them. The wood was sound. The varnish had not lifted. The strings pulled at the right tension. In the end she turned on the glue itself, laid on too thickly, holding the soundboard back from its own vibration. To test the idea she made up sample panels, hung each one from a thread, and tapped it. The heavily glued ones answered with a dull thud, the lighter ones rang out. So she thinned her mixture, warmed it gently, and called back every instrument she had already handed over. Her customers heard the change at the first playing. She now teaches the method to apprentices who travel a long way for it.

units: the narrator compared two recorded versions of the same set of pieces
the two listenings were a week apart
the first group takes a fast and very confident pace
that first version ends up wearing the listener out
the second group slows down and blends the tones more
one passage of the fast version is out of tune between two instruments
one piece of the slow version loses its coherence
the narrator picks the second version
his reason is that it stands up to repeated listening
text: I listened to two recordings of the same set of string pieces, a week apart, and honestly the gap between them threw me. The first group plays fast, with a swagger you can hear in every attack, right down to the players breathing. Brilliant stuff, and wearing after a while, like a light too bright to look at for long. The second group takes its time. Tempos stretch out, the tones melt into one another, and what sounded angular turns round. The first record grabbed me. This one kept me. Neither is spotless. On the fast one, a middle passage goes sour because the viola and the cello never quite agree. On the slow one, a single piece sags and loses the thread. Asked which of the two I would keep, I say the second without pausing, because it survives a replay and the fatigue never arrives before the end.

units: the writer is staying in a rented house beside an estuary
he chooses to describe the sounds rather than the views
the water strikes the supports of the building at a steady beat
the boats scrape when the level rises
a bird lets out an evening call he takes for a creaking door
human noises come from the quay and from a radio set
the wooden frame creaks during the night
those creaks make up a kind of tune
the writer records what he notices with the hour and the wind
he means to play his recordings when he gets back
text: I am writing from the low house we have rented near the estuary, and what I want to hand over to you here is what I hear, rather than what I see. Begin with the water: a steady slap against the posts under the floor, then the scrape of hulls as the rising tide lifts them straight. Then the birds. One of them lets out a thin call at dusk that I still take for a door swinging on a dry hinge. Then the people: voices carrying up from the quay, a radio playing somewhere far off, a cart rolling over the boards. The last one caught me off guard. The timbers themselves creak after dark, and the creaking settles into something close to a tune. I am writing it all down in a notebook, with the hour and the wind behind it. Once we are back home, I will play you the takes that came out well.

units: the origin of the phenomenon is older than the keeper can remember
her grandmother already knew this echo
the first returning sound she caught seemed weakened to her
she first put the cause down to the wind
she then suspected the work of water on the rock
a specialist in rocks explained to her the part played by the shape of the ground
she accepts that explanation and still comes to listen
the curious go away pleased once they have shouted
she waits until she is alone to say a short sentence
the voice that comes back to her sounds lower and altered
text: When did the cliff first answer? The keeper of the path waves the question off: the thing was there before she was born, and her grandmother knew it as a girl. What did she hear the first night? A call that came back to her worn thin, as if the rock gave it up unwillingly. Did she look for a reason? She blamed the wind, then the water that eats at the face, until a passing student of rocks spoke to her about the curve of the hollow. What does she do with that answer? She keeps it, and she still climbs up alone at dusk to hear her own voice return to her deeper than she sent it. And the visitors? They shout, they laugh, they go home pleased. She waits for them to walk off, then says a short sentence and lets the wall hand it back, rough and slightly changed, and she goes down telling nobody.

units: the technical manager explained the source of the shrill noise to the performer
the microphone was picking up the sound coming out of the speakers
that sound went back into the circuit and built itself up

the technician answered that the aim of the microphone weighed more
he advised moving the speakers behind the performer
he offered to cut the high frequencies and the input level
he recommended never aiming the microphone at a speaker
the test worked apart from a brief moment during a move toward the audience
text: The stage manager took the singer aside to explain where the shriek was coming from. Her microphone, he said, was picking up the speakers set out in front of her, that sound went back into the amplifier, and the loop fed itself until it howled. She asked whether the volume alone was to blame. Not really, he told her. Where the microphone points matters more, because a capsule aimed at a speaker hears its own echo. So what could be done? Move the speakers behind her, he suggested, pull down the high frequencies that flare up first, and take a little off the input as well. He added one rule for the stage: never swing the microphone toward a source, not even while bowing. The singer tried it through the sound check. The shriek stayed away, apart from one second, when she leaned out over the hall.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: passing melodies on by ear made them drift from one relay to the next
learning went by copying a sung model
after three relays two neighboring groups sang differently
the first scribes wrote signs above the sung words
those signs showed the direction of the voice but not the gap between the notes
you still had to know the tune to read those signs
the answer was to draw reference lines
the height of the sign then showed the pitch of the note
a performer could from then on sing a piece he had never heard
that invention opened the way to writing for several voices
text: Handing a melody down from one generation to the next raised a problem that memory alone could not settle. Singers learned by copying a model they had heard, and every copy drifted a little from the one before it. Three hands along, two settlements side by side no longer sang the same tune. The earliest copyists tried marks above the words, sketching where the voice rose and where it fell, without saying by how much. That helped, but not enough: you had to know the melody already before the marks meant anything. The answer turned out to be a plain piece of drawing. Rule one line across the page, then a second, and set each mark at a height you can measure. From then on the space of the page stood for the pitch of the sound. A singer could work out a tune he had never heard, and writing for several voices at once became possible.

units: in air the particles are far apart and carry the vibration poorly
sound fades quickly as it travels through air
in water the packed particles pass the vibration on with no delay
the vibration moves much faster in water than in air
a swimmer under the surface cannot tell where an engine noise comes from
that confusion comes from the signal reaching both ears too close together
metal carries the vibration better still than water
a wall of wool soaks up almost all of the vibration
the same blow gives a different sound depending on what carries it
text: Put two ways of carrying a sound side by side. In air the wave spreads out fast: the molecules sit far apart, they hand the shock along lazily, and the message fades within a short distance. In water those same molecules almost touch. The shock passes from one to the next with no delay, and sound travels far quicker there than it does through air. That is why a diver hears a distant engine yet cannot tell where it lies: the signal reaches both of his ears too soon for him to compare them. The comparison holds for solids too. A steel bar carries a vibration better still than water does, while a wall of wool soaks up nearly all of it. One blow struck on those three gives three results: a bright crack on the metal, a dull ringing under water, a short flat thud in the wool.

units: the narrator expected a long session but not a failed one

she refused to soften her part in spite of it
noisy building work broke into a quiet passage

the final result turned out to be good
the musicians kept those choices for the performance
text: They warned me the run-through would drag on. Nobody warned me it would turn into a run of disasters. First blow: the pianist shows up with a bandaged finger and announces he will play with the left hand only. Second blow: the room, lent to us by a dance school, has a floor that throws everything back, so the smallest note cracks and returns doubled. Third blow: the singer has caught a cold, her voice comes out raw, and she flatly refuses to lighten her part. Fourth blow, the best of them: somebody drills through the shared wall during the quietest passage. We kept going out of sheer stubbornness. And the thing held up. That left hand laid down a rocking bass none of us had imagined, the ragged voice fit the words, and the floor pushed us to play softer than usual. On the night, we asked for rugs and kept it all.
